messages.body_plain:
Distorted markers should be removed cause it can lead to non causal or wrong statistical significance in QTL detection...

Single marker always should be done... The problem related to single marker QTL analyses it that the causal gene, most of the times, isn't the analysed marker. This fact happens, for exemple, when we consider genetic markers just like SSR, that for sure we know isn't a codant region. Significance in most cases is related to linkage effect between the analysed marker and the causal gene.

Most of the times, single marker analyses is pretty importante when we procede analyses just like CIM or procedure when we need associated markers as covariates, and they could be chosen taking a look at the results of single marker analyse...

It would be helpfull if someone could add some information or correct if I wrote something wrong or missplaced...
I'm sorry for my English...

Best Regards
Rafael

messages.body_plain:
Is it an isolated marker showing segregation distortion which all surrounding markers look fine (that would indicate genotyping error), or does an entire chromosome region show distortion in the same way (that would seem to be real).

In QTL mapping, we condition on the observed genotypes, so results are usually not much affected by real distortion, though can be some loss of power if some genotypes are only observed in a few individuals.

karl

I do not wish to start a new map from scratch using both the high and low quality markers but rather somehow add the new markers into a final map that was produced using only the high quality markers.

My issue begins with the fact that the new markers are not present in the original input file that I used to make the final map, and I am unsure of how to add this data while maintaining the final order of the original markers. Do you have any recommendations on how to approach this in an efficient manner?

I would really appreciate any advice.

Thank you for your time.

Best,
Lucydalila

est.map can be run using multiple processors in parallel, one for each chromosome, using the 'n.cluster' argument.

I would generally run such long-running R jobs from the command-line: put the R commands into a script file, say "myscript.R" and then type

  R CMD BATCH myscript.R

You can estimate the map for a single chromosome at a time and combine them using c(). And you can use replacemap() with a map for just one or a few chromosomes.

  data(hyper)
  map1 <- est.map(hyper, chr=1)
  map2 <- est.map(hyper, chr=2)
  map1n2 <- c(map1, map2)
  hyper <- replacemap(hyper, map1n2)

In a phase known 4-way cross, the four grandparents are labeled A, B, C, and D, with one parent being AxB and the other CxD. At a fully informative marker, the offspring would have genotypes AC, AD, BC, or BD. But with typical markers, not all four alleles can be distinguished. You need to know "phase" (that is, which allele came from which grandparent), and then at each marker code the genotypes using numbers 1-14:  1 = AC, 2 = BC, 3 = AD, 4 = BD, 5 = A = AC or AD, 6 = B = BC or BD, 7 = C = AC or BC, 8 = D = AD or BD, 9 = AC or BD, 10 = AD or BC, 11 = not AC, 12 = not BC, 13 = not AD, 14 = not BD.

Then in the read.cross function, use the argument genotypes=1:14

karl

  library(qtl)

  out_c1 <- scanone(hyper_c1)
  out_c2 <- scanone(hyper_c2)
  out <- rbind(out_c1, out_c2)

messages.body_plain:
Ideally use an assumed genotyping error rate that approximately matches the actual error rate.

It generally has little influence on the inference of marker order, but can affect the estimates of inter-marker distances. I had generally used 0.01 for old low-density microsat data and am now generally using 0.002 for SNP arrays, but I've not worked with GBS data directly. I'd try out different values and see how different the results are. And you can in principle estimate the error rate. See pg 35 of the genetic map construction tutorial: http://rqtl.org/tutorials/geneticmaps.pdf
